client: I've been really struggling lately with this overwhelming dread about my final exams coming up next month. After how badly last term went for me, I just keep imagining the worst — like I'm going to fail everything and ruin my future. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the exams are still going to be there no matter what we discuss.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy weight right now — that dread about exams layered on top of the pain from last term, and then on top of *that*, a worry that even reaching out for help might not make a difference. That last part stands out to me, because it takes real courage to show up even when a part of you feels like it might be pointless. I'm curious — when you imagine the worst happening, what does that story usually sound like in your head?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: When I imagine the worst, it's like this whole chain reaction plays out — I fail the exams, I lose my scholarship, I have to drop out, and then I'm just... stuck, like I've completely wasted my chance at a real future. It's almost like my brain won't let me stop at just "doing badly on a test," it has to go all the way to the most catastrophic version of events. And the worst part is it feels so real and so certain, not like a worry but like something I already know is going to happen.
therapist: What you're describing — that mental spiral that races from one exam all the way to "my entire future is ruined" — is something we call catastrophic thinking, and the fact that it *feels* like certainty rather than fear is actually one of the most exhausting parts of it. Your voice and your words are both telling me how urgent and real this feels right now, like your mind is running at full speed trying to brace for impact. I'd love to gently slow that chain down with you — when you look at the very first link, failing the exams, what actual evidence do you have for and against that happening?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I mean, I guess the evidence against it is that I didn't fail everything last term — I did badly in two subjects but I still passed the others. But it's hard to hold onto that because the two I struggled with feel so much louder than the ones I managed okay, and I keep thinking last term was actually me getting lucky rather than me actually being capable. I don't know if looking at evidence is really going to quiet that voice, because it feels like the voice has a counter-argument for everything.
therapist: You just did something really important — you found real evidence, and then immediately watched your mind try to take it away by calling it "luck." That pattern has a name: it's called discounting the positive, and it's incredibly common, but it's also worth noticing that the evidence *is* there whether the voice accepts it or not. I'm curious — if a close friend told you they passed most of their exams but struggled in two, would you tell them they just got lucky, or would you see it differently?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, no, I wouldn't say that to a friend — I'd probably tell them they clearly have some ability and just need to work on the weaker areas. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself it just... doesn't land the same way, it feels almost dishonest, like I'm trying to trick myself into feeling better rather than seeing things clearly. I think part of me is scared that if I stop being so hard on myself, I'll get complacent and then I really will fail.
therapist: That fear — that self-compassion equals giving up — is such a common trap, and it's worth gently challenging: has being hard on yourself actually *prevented* you from struggling, or has it mostly just made the struggling feel more unbearable? The way you described it, almost quietly, like you were admitting something vulnerable, makes me think part of you already senses that the harshness isn't really protecting you. What do you think it would actually look like to hold yourself to high standards *without* the cruelty?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, being hard on myself hasn't stopped me from struggling — last term I was incredibly self-critical the whole time and it didn't make me study better, it just made me feel paralyzed and awful. But I genuinely don't know what high standards without the cruelty even looks like in practice, because in my head they've always been the same thing — like the pressure is what's supposed to push me forward. I'm not sure I'd even recognize a kinder version of motivation if I saw it, or trust that it would actually work for me.
therapist: You just made a really significant connection — that the self-criticism didn't drive you forward, it froze you — and that's not a small thing to recognize. I notice you're speaking quite quickly and softly, like there's a lot rushing through you right now, and I want to make sure we sit with what you just said, because it's important: you already *know* the cruelty isn't working. I'm wondering — can you think of any time in your life, even outside of academics, where you felt genuinely motivated by something that felt encouraging rather than punishing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Actually, yeah — there was this one time in high school where I had a art teacher who genuinely seemed to believe I was talented, and I worked so much harder in that class than any other, not because I was scared of failing but because I wanted to live up to what she saw in me. But that feels like a really long time ago and a completely different context, and I'm not sure how I'm supposed to recreate that feeling on my own when there's no one around who believes in me like that right now. It's hard because back then the encouragement was coming from outside — I don't know how to be that for myself.
therapist: That memory is actually really precious evidence — it shows you *know* what it feels like to be motivated by belief rather than fear, which means that capacity lives in you, even if it feels distant right now. What's striking is that your art teacher didn't create your talent, she just *reflected back* what was already there — and I wonder if part of this work is learning to be that witness for yourself. What do you think she saw in you back then that you have the hardest time seeing in yourself now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think she saw someone who was persistent and genuinely cared about doing things well, who would keep trying even when something wasn't working out right away. But honestly, when I try to see that in myself now, it just feels like I'm making things up — like I've lost whatever that quality was, or maybe it only existed in a context where someone else was validating it. And that's kind of a scary thought, that maybe I can't function well without external approval, which makes me feel even more alone going into these exams.
therapist: The qualities you just described — persistence, genuinely caring, keep trying even when it's hard — you demonstrated all of those *right here*, in this conversation, working through something really difficult even when part of you didn't think it would help. I also notice something tender in the way you said that, like you're grieving a version of yourself you're not sure still exists, and I want to gently push back: what if that quality didn't disappear, but just got buried under all the self-criticism we've been talking about? It might be worth asking — is there anything in how you've shown up today, or even last term, that that persistent, caring person would recognize as her own?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess... showing up here today, even when I was convinced it wouldn't help, is maybe something that person would recognize. And last term, even when things were falling apart, I did keep going to most of my classes and I didn't completely give up, even though it felt like I was barely holding on. But I'm worried that if I start framing those things as signs of strength, I'm setting myself up for a bigger crash when the exams actually arrive and things go wrong again.
therapist: You just did it again — found real evidence and then immediately braced against it, as if allowing yourself to feel encouraged is the dangerous part. But here's something worth sitting with: recognizing your own strength isn't a prediction that everything will go perfectly, it's just an accurate account of who you've already shown yourself to be under pressure. What if the goal isn't to guarantee a good outcome, but to face whatever happens with someone in your corner — even if that someone is you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That idea of being in my own corner is... actually kind of moving to hear, but it also feels really foreign, almost like you're describing a relationship I don't know how to have with myself. I think the honest truth is that I don't fully trust myself — like, if I'm in my own corner, what happens when I let myself down, which feels inevitable with these exams? It's scary to rely on myself as a source of support when I've also been the main source of all this criticism.
therapist: What you just said — that the critic and the support would have to come from the same place — that's one of the most honest and courageous things you've shared today, and I can hear how much weight is behind it. Being in your own corner doesn't mean never letting yourself down, it means that when you do, you respond with understanding rather than attack — the same way you'd show up for that friend who passed most of their exams. I'm wondering, what would it feel like to experiment with just that — not trusting yourself perfectly, but committing to not abandoning yourself when things get hard?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That framing actually feels a little more manageable than what I thought you were going to suggest, because it's not asking me to suddenly believe in myself completely, just to not make things worse by turning on myself. But I'm still not sure what that looks like practically when I'm in the middle of a panic at 2am before an exam and my brain is just spiraling — like, the intention sounds good here in this room, but I don't know if I'll have access to it in that moment. What would that even look like, not abandoning myself, when everything feels like it's falling apart?
therapist: That's exactly the right question to ask, because insight in a calm moment and access to it at 2am are genuinely different challenges — and it's wise that you're already thinking ahead to that gap. One practical anchor could be something as simple as a single sentence you write to yourself *now*, in this clearer headspace, that your panicking self can find later — something like "you're still here, you're still trying, that's enough for tonight." Would it feel worth trying to put that into your own words, something that sounds like *you* being in your corner rather than abandoning yourself when it gets dark?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
